chunks: "The difference is where the extra voltage goes. An LDO is basically a controlled resistor in series with the load. To drop 12 volts to 3. 3 volts at 2 amps, it has to drop the 8.
7 volts difference across the pass transistor while carrying the full 2 amps, so it burns 8. 7 volts times 2 amps, 17 watts, to deliver 6. 6 watts.
Efficiency is just V out over V in , 27%. The input current is also 2 amps, because the same current flows through it.
A buck never lets the excess voltage sit across something carrying current.
The switch is either fully on, so it has almost no voltage across it, or fully off, so it has no current. An ideal switch dissipates nothing.
The inductor and capacitor store energy and give it back, so they don't dissipate either.
What the buck does is chop the input into pulses and let the LC filter average them, so the output is D times V in .
Energy is conserved, so an ideal buck takes input current of only D times I out , here 0. 55 amps instead of 2 amps.
In a real buck you lose a few percent in switch resistance, switching transitions, inductor resistance and gate drive, so you get 90 to 95% instead of 27%, about 0.
5 watts of heat instead of 17 watts. The LDO still has a place: when V in is only slightly above V out , at very light loads, or where you need low noise."
